segments.description: Please join me in welcoming Luke Vella to the Grand Slam Coaches Conference. Luke is a strength and conditioning coach with over 15 years of experience in elite and professional sport. He has coached athletes in both Olympic and professional team sports and is currently the head of strength and conditioning for the Melbourne Rebels Super Rugby franchise. Luke has a PhD in exercise and nutrition science from the Deakin University and has a long-standing passion in injury rehabilitation. Today Luke shares some practices in strength and conditioning for long-term athletic development in junior players. Over to you Luke. Good morning everyone my name is Luke Vella and I'm the current head of performance at the Melbourne Rebels. I want to take the opportunity to thank Paul and Simon for the invitation to speak to you today. It's a privilege to be a part of this conference. This morning I'm going to speak to you a little bit about my experience as a strength and conditioning coach working in junior athlete development across a range of different sports including junior tennis and more specifically the impact that growth, maturation and the relative age effect can have on athlete management. I will start by talking a little bit about my background and how my principles and philosophies surrounding long-term athletic development have evolved. I'll then delve into a phenomenon that exists across world sport known as the

relative age effect and the impact that it's having on junior tennis. I'll talk about my experiences around using growth and maturation status as a key measure of athletic development and how we've used this idea to inform training and competition from both a technical, tactical and physical perspective. Then finally I look to introduce this concept of bio-banding which is an idea developed originally in English Premier League football which I believe has a big future in junior sport. My career as an S&C coach started back in 2007, possibly showing my age a little bit with the Collingwood football club followed by a stint with St Kilder in 2012. My first exposure to tennis as an S&C coach was back in 2009 where I had the opportunity to work alongside the great Paul Akin with two Melbourne based New Zealand brothers Ruben and Oliver Staven. I then ventured north to the UK where I worked out at the University of Bath and it was here that I had the opportunity to meet to meet these two people here in the centre of the screen. The gentleman on the left is Sean Cumming. Sean is a world-leading practitioner in the world of junior athlete development and the role of maturation on sporting and athletic performance. Sean's worked very closely with the English Premier League football academies and developed systems and infrastructures that promote participation and performance in sport. The lady on the right is Corinne

Yolston who at the time was a PhD candidate and her PhD research into the methods to quantify junior athletes at different stages of maturity has played a big role in influencing my opinions in this area. I then decided to go a little further north to Edinburgh for four years to work with Scottish rugby which eventually led me back home to my current role with the Melbourne rebels. From an education side I've completed all of my studies at Deakin University starting with a bachelor's degree in exercise and nutrition science and finishing with a PhD that took the better part of ten years and if anyone's having any difficulty falling asleep later tonight I'll be happy to share the details of my PhD with you. So the relative age effect for those of you that haven't come across this term before is the concept that athletes who are born earlier in the calendar year are more likely to be successful and progress through the development pathways of their chosen sport. This concept is likely due to the relative age and maturity difference especially in the early junior ranks of sport. You can see in the diagram on the right here we have two under 13 junior rugby players in South Africa. One of these boys is weighing in at 102 kilos and the other at 39 kilos demonstrating the difference in maturity levels for junior athletes of the same chronological age. What the research tells us is that this concept is prevalent in the world of junior tennis with a chart on

the left from a study back in 2005 showing more than double the population of junior tennis players who would progress through to the elite level were born in the first quarter of the calendar year relative to the fourth quarter. So the relative age effect looks at differences in sporting prowess based on chronological age. If we were to pivot on this and look at progressions through junior development pathways based on the rate at which junior athletes mature the impact of the relative age effect is likely to be much greater. What you see on the right here is a typical growth curve for a male and a female. The yellow and red lines demonstrate the rate at which the individual is growing referred to as peak height velocity. What this chart shows us and as we already know girls reflected in yellow will typically achieve their growth spurt earlier than boys in red. However the magnitude of this growth is typically greater in boys reflected by the blue and green lines respectively. So as we know children will grow and mature at different rates. I myself am still waiting for my growth spurt that my parents promised me over 20 years ago. What we can see on this chart on the right is a hypothetical comparison between three individuals compared based on their growth per year. During my time in the UK the LTA had a big focus on developing the current crop of players in the under 14 age group. If we were to compare these three

individuals at 14 years of age from a developmental perspective we would see that individual A is 16 years of age, individual B is 14 and individual C is only 12 years of age. In this instance we'd refer to individual A as an early mature and individual C as a late mature. However in the current format where competition is based on chronological age and selection into development pathways is based on chronological age all three of these individuals would be forced to train and compete against one another. Now in the world of tennis it's not difficult to see and understand how individual A is going to be at a considerable advantage. Bigger bodies will typically mean bigger serves, perhaps more power off the ground and more development from a physical perspective is going to lend itself to better court coverage. So some key things that we're able to identify within the research. Firstly we know that early maturing athletes are typically more developed physically, technically and tactically. If we look purely at physical performance we know that physical performance is directly correlated with biological maturity. We also know that early maturing athletes are more likely to be selected in talent identification scores and this is regardless of sport this is across contact sports, non-contact sports, team sports, individual sports. We know that when looking at the relative age effects when it's considered in terms of relative maturity it is much

greater than when we consider it as relative birth date or chronological age. Now the caveat to all of this is we also know that maturity status and youth talent has no predictive value towards senior excellence. So what this means is if we look at the number of people who progress through junior talent development pathways and we look at the number of those who go on to senior careers in professional or high-level sport, those that mature later tend to have more success than their early maturing counterparts. So this begs the question if in our development pathways we are unconsciously prioritizing those who mature earlier, is this current system doing a disservice to late maturers and is there a better way that we can encourage participation in sport across different levels of maturity and also promote the development both technically, tactically and physically of junior athletes across the maturation spectrum. And this is where the concept of measuring and quantifying a junior athlete's maturity status has evolved from. Previously we used to have to complete a series of bone scans and measure skeletal growth as our gold standard measure of maturity. However now things are much simpler. During my time in the UK I was fortunate enough to work in Southampton's Football Academy for a very brief period of time and it was here where I was introduced to the CAMIS Roche method where maturity status can be calculated from five simple

variables. A mother's and father's height, the child's height, the child's weight and the child's age. From these numbers we're able to calculate an individual's percentage of peak adult stature and what we know is that across the spectrum of peak adult stature will be certain developmental milestones. For example we know that at approximately 89% of peak adult stature is when an individual typically experienced their growth spurt. Using these types of methods, very smart people like Dr. Sean Cumming were able to create this idea of biobanding where junior athletes were put into bins or categories based on where they were on this developmental spectrum. Initially this started out as a strategy to move particular athletes temporarily to train either up or down an age group based on their maturation status alongside input from their coaches and parents about whether there might be developmental opportunities for them to train alongside athletes of a similar maturity level. However this concept has now evolved into the Premier League hosting tournaments where junior athletes compete in teams based on the level of physical maturity rather than based on their chronological age. So why would we consider using biobanding? Well there are three primary reasons as to why grouping players for training and competition purposes based on their level of maturity has the potential to benefit athletic development. First and foremost if we consider talent

identification. In the majority of sports across the world there will be physical stands that are considered important to the sport and at the top level there will be benchmarks that junior athletes will be encouraged to achieve. These will typically be a measure of strength, a measure of speed and possibly a measure of fitness. However we know that from our example previously that not all for example 14 year olds are well 14 years old. So why would we be expecting and encouraging them to achieve physical milestones at the same time? Secondary to that we know that at different stages of maturity we're going to encounter different physical development, call them hurdles. The most popular of these is the adolescent awkwardness phase. This typically occurs at about 89% of peak adult stature or right about the time of peak height velocity. Two fancy terms for the growth spurt. During this time we're inevitably going to see a reduction in certain physical performance characteristics that are influenced by coordination and relative muscle strength. Therefore it makes sense that if we're going to create physical targets for junior athletes to try to achieve and base certain elements of our talent identification on these physical standards then it should be considered relative to the individual's physical developmental trajectory. Likewise when we look at certain sports that might have

recruitment trials we're likely to encounter scenarios where early maturing athletes are able to rely on their physical dominance. However this may not necessarily reflect tactical or technical proficiency. In this instance it's not unrealistic to explore the idea that a late maturing 13 or 14 year old misses out on selection into a team or a squad, becomes discouraged, loses confidence and stops participating. The second example here is in the prescription of strength and conditioning programs. We know that at different stages of development the skeletal muscle system and the neuromuscular system are going to adapt and respond to different forms of training. We're going to have windows of time where the body is going to be more responsive to speed training for example and this will also be the same for strength and fitness qualities and I'll touch on these a little bit more later on. We also know that there are going to be times such as during adolescence awkwardness. The junior athletes are going to be more susceptible to injury if their training schedules are not managed appropriately. During this time coordination of fundamental movement patterns is likely to be inhibited and growth related over training injuries are the potential result. By understanding and pre-empting when this is going to occur, coaches, strength and conditioners and medical staff can be prepared to intervene or

even act proactively to help the athlete develop throughout this stage. And finally, competition. The concept that an early maturing athlete can rely on their physical dominance to be successful in junior sport is detrimental for several reasons. Firstly, and as we've already discussed, the opportunity for late maturing players to participate and be competitive is considerably limited because they're at such a physical disadvantage. This is particularly true for the sport that I'm now working in in the world of rugby where Beth Dowling, a former master's student at La Trobe, has just finished a terrific thesis identifying the relative age effect in Victorian rugby union. The other downside is that early maturing athletes are also missing an opportunity to be challenged from a technical and tactical perspective because they're able to leverage their physical attributes to dominate the sport. Once everyone reaches maturity and they're no longer able to rely on their physical dominance, this missed opportunity to be challenged may be a key reason why dominance in junior levels of sport is not necessarily strongly correlated to senior sporting excellence. So considering the challenges we encounter using chronological age for physical profiling and talent identification, here we have an example of two athletes who have undergone a series of physical tests. The blue bars represent their

performance relative to their chronological age while the orange bars represent performance relative to their level of maturity. The data is displayed as Z scores from the average with the centre line zero point being the group average. As we can see from the top two bars, the athlete on the left is relatively much smaller and we know that this individual is considered a late maturer. Contrastingly, the athlete on the right is much, much bigger and we know that this athlete is classified as an early maturer. As we scroll down the page, we see that relative to their chronological age, the athlete on the left has performed quite poorly with the vast majority of their performances living below the average with the exception of counter movement jump height. When compared to his or her maturational age, they actually perform quite well with the majority of their metrics living above the average, in particular around jump height and speed. Contrastingly, the athlete on the right, our early maturing athlete, performs well above the average on all metrics when compared to others of the same chronological age. However, when compared to athletes of the same level of maturity, we see that the vast majority of these metrics now fall below the midline, suggesting that their physical testing profile is actually below average for their level of development. So when considering the physical testing profile for both of

these individuals, compared to chronological age, it could be mistaken for thinking that our late maturing athlete on the left here is well behind in his physical development, whereas our early maturing athlete would be considered much further advanced. However, if we consider these two individuals relative to their level of maturity, we can see that our late maturing athlete is actually outperforming our early maturing athlete and is likely to potentially go on to achieve greater levels of physical development. Elaborating a little bit more on the manipulation of strength and conditioning programs during different stages of growth and maturation, we can see from these two diagrams on the right that throughout the process of maturation, we encounter different windows of opportunity for physical development. It's important to understand that these windows are simply an indication of when the neuromuscular system is going to be most sensitive to adapting to certain physical training methods and a holistic and well-rounded strength and conditioning program will always be encouraged. So we can see that during the pre-puberty window, we're going to see a window for speed development, suppleness, which incorporates mobility and flexibility and not surprisingly skill development. During peak height velocity, we might encounter the adolescent awkwardness phase, which means that motor control and coordination will likely need to be addressed. We will

also see a secondary speed window and an opportunity to develop and challenge certain fitness qualities. Post peak height velocity and certainly not surprisingly, this is when we start to see our opportunity of strength and conditioning coaches to start to target improvements in maximal strength. It's during this window that many S&C coaches will start to work off the principle that the ability to generate high amounts of force or show good levels of strength will underpin improvements in other physical qualities such as speed and power development. When considering load management and injury risk, particularly during the peak height velocity phase, it's important to remember that each of your athletes will respond to growth very differently. Some will encounter significant reductions in their physical performance and coordination, while others will coast through this phase largely unfazed. In any sense, clarity on when you are likely to encounter this phase will prepare you to intervene appropriately depending on what you encounter. All modifications and discussions around training load management must be interdisciplinary in nature and involve inputs from technical coaching staff along with the S&C and medical teams. Okay, so to summarize some of my key points from this presentation. Firstly, the relative age effect is real. Athletes who are born earlier in the calendar year or mature earlier than

their peers are at a distinct advantage when it comes to junior sport. The dark side of this is that there is a whole population of junior athletes who are at a disadvantage and likely missing out on coaching and development opportunities. Likewise, our early maturers who might be enjoying the free ride coasting on the back of growing facial hair first are not being challenged whether that be tactically, technically or even psychologically to ensure that their dominance over the rest of the field carries over to the high levels of senior sport. Secondly, using maturation status to quantify development should be used as a monitoring tool for your athletes. Different developmental milestones occur at the same stage of maturity for all of us. Measuring it is uninvasive, relatively time and cost effective and provides vital information in helping you understand your athletes better. We know there's still no golden nugget of information that tells us everything we need to know and there will always be a level of individuality to how athletes are affected by maturation, but this is a vital piece of information in understanding junior athlete development. My third point here is that biobanding has the potential to create a unique training environment to improve and equal opportunities for all junior athletes to train and compete. It has benefits for both early and late maturing athletes alike to compete and be

challenged on a more level playing field. And finally, perhaps more a statement from my own personal philosophy in coaching junior athletes. They are not many versions of senior athletes that we coach. They're evolving. One day they're talking about pool patrol. Then they want their own phones and nothing to do with their parents. The more we can understand about the physical challenges of maturation that they're likely to encounter, the better our capacity as coaches to adapt, support and meet these junior athletes where they're at. That is all from me for now. Again, massive thanks to Paul and Simon for the opportunity and the invitation to come and present to you today. I'm always very happy to be contacted either via email or LinkedIn or any social media platforms that I'm not really on too much, but happy to answer any questions that might come off the back of this and I'm keen to keep talking about all things junior athlete development. Thank you very much.
